sections.content: You know *la subida de los precios* from B2 Unit 21: *nominalización* turns an action into a noun and leaves the doer out. Administrations overuse it. *Se procedió a la realización de la revisión* has three nouns and no real verb for a simple fact: someone reviewed something. The plain version keeps the *se* and puts the action back into the verb: *Se revisó*. At C1 you need both skills: to read the dense version without getting lost, and to write the short version when the reader is a citizen. A short verb tells who or what is affected and when. A chain of nouns hides it.

sections.title: From dense to plain
rows: Se procedió a la realización de la revisión del expediente.
Se efectuará el pago de la tasa.
Se llevará a cabo la simplificación del trámite.
Se procederá a la tramitación de las solicitudes.

items.spanish: Se revisó el expediente y se otorgó la licencia.
items.english: The file was reviewed and the licence was granted.

items.spanish: Se pagará la tasa en línea.
items.english: The fee will be paid online.

items.spanish: El nuevo trámite ha agilizado el procedimiento.
items.english: The new procedure has speeded up the process.

items.spanish: La jerga hace más lenta la burocracia.

sections.content: English advice to "use plain words" works in Spanish too, but the pull is stronger because nouns in *-ción* come so easily. Test a sentence: if the main verb is only *proceder a*, *efectuar* or *llevar a cabo*, look for the noun after it and turn it back into a verb. Keep the long form only when a formal text really needs it, such as a regulation (see C1 Unit 6).
